editorial_sections.h2: How to type special characters anywhere
paragraphs: There are several ways to insert a special character, but copy and paste is the fastest and the most reliable across devices:

Because these characters are part of Unicode, they display consistently on iPhone, Android, Windows, and Mac. A handful of the rarer mathematical and decorative glyphs can fall back to a missing-character box on older systems; if that happens, choose a more common alternative from the same category. Boxes on a perfectly good character are a missing-font problem, explained in why text shows as boxes.

editorial_sections.h2: Which Field Actually Accepts Special Characters
paragraphs: The most common reason a special character “won’t save” is that it went into the wrong field. Nearly every platform splits your identity into two separate names, and only one of them accepts these characters:
Platform specifics, each verified separately: Instagram, Discord, and the field-by-field breakdown of which Discord surface takes what.

Games set their own rules. Many titles allow Latin characters only and reject the rest outright, and a rename often costs money or a token. Paste your text into the field and let the game validate it before you commit.
Want a name that looks empty rather than decorated? A plain space gets trimmed and rejected: you need a character that is not classified as whitespace. See invisible characters.

A special character is any symbol outside the basic letters (A–Z, a–z) and digits (0–9). That includes punctuation like & and @, currency marks like € and £, math signs like ∞ and ±, and decorative glyphs like ★ and ✧. All of them are part of Unicode.
Just click the symbol you want on this page: it copies to your clipboard instantly, then paste it with Ctrl + V (Windows) or Cmd + V (Mac). You never need to remember a numeric code.

That happens when the app or device doesn't have a font glyph for that specific character. It's a display issue, not a copy error: the character is still correct underneath. Switching to a more widely supported symbol from the same category usually fixes it.

Special punctuation (! @ # $ % & *) strengthens passwords and is widely accepted. Rarer Unicode symbols, however, are often rejected by username and password fields, so stick to common ASCII punctuation there and save the decorative glyphs for posts and bios.

[OBJ] is a placeholder some Android apps and older messaging clients show when they can't render a specific emoji or Unicode character: short for "object replacement." The character itself was copied and sent correctly; the receiving app just doesn't have a glyph for it yet. It's the text-mode version of the missing-character box above, and it typically resolves once the app or OS updates its font and emoji set.

Anything beyond letters, digits and the punctuation printed on the keys: hearts (♥ ♡), stars (★ ☆), ticks (✓ ✔), arrows (→ ←), infinity (∞), degree (°) and most currency marks. They exist in Unicode, they just have no key, so copying is the fastest way to use them.
Tap ♥ or ♡ above. Unlike the emoji on a phone keyboard, these are text characters: they take the colour and size of the surrounding text and work in username fields and forms that reject emoji.
